# Periodic but not circular: a 24-hour activity rhythm

Suppose an activity sensor reports a continuous level between 0 and 1, with small values indicating little activity and large values indicating much more. We want to describe how that level changes over the day. Time of day repeats: midnight at the end of one day returns to the same position in the daily cycle. Activity does not wrap around in this way. An activity level near 0 is very different from one near 1.

This distinction determines the model. A circular likelihood such as the von Mises describes an angular response, where a full turn returns to the same outcome. Here the response is a bounded activity level, so we use a Beta likelihood for values strictly between 0 and 1. The daily rhythm enters through the predictors. Using a periodic predictor does not require the response itself to be circular.

There are two questions to answer: how does average activity change through the day, and how variable are observations made at the same time? We allow the Beta mean and precision to have separate daily patterns. The example uses simulated observations so that we know the patterns that generated them and can compare those patterns with the fitted model.

## Figure style

Time runs from 0 to 24 hours along the horizontal axis. On an activity axis, vertical distance is an ordinary difference in activity: the top and bottom of that scale are distinct outcomes, even though the two ends of the time axis represent the same daily phase.


## 1. Simulate the 24-hour rhythm

We generate 1,000 independent observations at evenly spaced times across a day. Their underlying mean and precision change smoothly with time; individual observations are drawn from the activity distribution at their respective times.

Let $\theta(t)=2\pi t/24$, with $t$ measured in hours. Sine and cosine return to their starting values after 24 hours. Combining them lets a daily peak occur at a time determined by their coefficients, rather than fixing it at the peak of either basis function. For this example, the two predictors are

$$
\eta_\mu(t)=0.5+2\sin\theta(t)+1.5\cos\theta(t),
\qquad
\eta_\phi(t)=2+\sin\theta(t)+0.5\cos\theta(t).
$$

We turn these into a valid mean and a positive precision using

$$
\mu(t)=\frac{1}{1+\exp[-\eta_\mu(t)]},
\qquad
\phi(t)=\log\!\left(1+\exp[\eta_\phi(t)]\right),
$$

then draw activity as

$$
y_i\sim\operatorname{Beta}\!\left(\mu(t_i)\phi(t_i),\,[1-\mu(t_i)]\phi(t_i)\right).
$$

The first transformation keeps the mean between 0 and 1; the second, called softplus, keeps precision positive. The predictors are sinusoidal, but the transformed mean and precision need not be sine waves. These chosen coefficients produce high mean activity early in the day and low mean activity in the afternoon.

The cycle length is fixed at 24 hours. Within each curve, its coefficients and the resulting peak time remain constant; the mean activity changes because time advances through the cycle. The mean and precision can peak at different hours because they have different coefficients. Both curves agree at 0 and 24 hours. Two observations at those endpoints can still differ, just as two observations at any other shared time can differ.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "periodic-not-circular-011"
set.seed(42)
num_points <- 1000L
time <- seq(0, 24, length.out = num_points)
sin24 <- sin(2 * pi * time / 24)
cos24 <- cos(2 * pi * time / 24)
mu_alpha_true <- 0.5
mu_sin_true <- 2.0
mu_cos_true <- 1.5
phi_alpha_true <- 2.0
phi_sin_true <- 1.0
phi_cos_true <- 0.5
mu_true <- plogis(mu_alpha_true + mu_sin_true * sin24 + mu_cos_true * cos24)
phi_true <- softplus_stable(phi_alpha_true + phi_sin_true * sin24 + phi_cos_true * cos24)
activity <- rbeta(num_points, mu_true * phi_true, (1 - mu_true) * phi_true)
# The continuous Beta outcome is in (0,1); guard finite-precision draws
# that round to an endpoint. The margin must also survive brms' JSON
# serialization to Stan (~15 significant figures), which would
# round 1 - 2^-52 to 1 and make the Beta likelihood -inf for all
# draws (every initial value rejected, no fit).
activity <- pmin(1 - 1e-10, pmax(1e-10, activity))
# EQUIVALENCE NOTE: same seed, distribution, grid, and truths as Python;
# R's rbeta and NumPy's beta sampler do not generate bit-identical values.
data <- data.frame(time, sin24, cos24, activity)
stopifnot(nrow(data) == 1000L, all(activity > 0 & activity < 1))
head(data)

```

## 2. Fit the periodic model

We now treat the six coefficients used to construct the two predictors as unknown. The fitted model has the same form as the simulation:

$$
\eta_\mu(t)=\beta_0+\beta_s\sin\theta(t)+\beta_c\cos\theta(t),
\qquad
\eta_\phi(t)=\alpha_0+\alpha_s\sin\theta(t)+\alpha_c\cos\theta(t).
$$

The observations inform the baseline level and the strength and timing of each daily pattern. The cycle length remains fixed at 24 hours. All six coefficients have independent Normal priors with standard deviation 1. In intercept, sine, cosine order, the prior means are $(0,2,2)$ for the mean predictor and $(1,1,0)$ for the precision predictor. These priors regularize the estimates. Several are centered above zero, so they favor some daily patterns over others before seeing the observations.

Precision describes variation among observations, not our uncertainty about a fitted coefficient. Its effect is easiest to see from

$$
\operatorname{Var}(y\mid t)=\frac{\mu(t)[1-\mu(t)]}{\phi(t)+1}.
$$

At a fixed mean, larger precision gives less variation. Across the day, both mean and precision change, so both contribute to changes in the spread of activity. Estimating these two patterns separately lets mean activity and precision peak at different times.

The coefficient summaries and trace panels help inspect the sampled estimates. The saved fit reports that divergence information was not retained, so these outputs do not provide a complete convergence assessment.

The following two curve panels separate the fitted mean activity from the fitted precision. Black lines are posterior averages of each underlying curve; orange ribbons are 95% highest-density intervals for that curve at each time. Dashed blue lines show the values used to simulate the observations. These ribbons describe uncertainty in the underlying mean or precision, rather than the range of possible individual activity observations.

The fitted curves reproduce the broad daily pattern, with some departures from the generating curves. In particular, the fitted precision peak is below the simulated peak. Compare both the locations of peaks and troughs and the differences in their heights.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "periodic-not-circular-013"
form <- bf(activity ~ 0 + Intercept + sin24 + cos24,
  nlf(phi ~ log(log1p_exp(eta))),
  eta ~ 0 + Intercept + sin24 + cos24,
  family = brms::Beta(link = "logit", link_phi = "log"))
priors <- (
  prior("normal(0, 1)", class = "b", coef = "Intercept") +
  prior("normal(2, 1)", class = "b", coef = "sin24") +
  prior("normal(2, 1)", class = "b", coef = "cos24") +
  prior("normal(1, 1)", class = "b", coef = "Intercept", nlpar = "eta") +
  prior("normal(1, 1)", class = "b", coef = "sin24", nlpar = "eta") +
  prior("normal(0, 1)", class = "b", coef = "cos24", nlpar = "eta")
)
ITER <- if (quick_run) 1500L else 2000L
WARMUP <- if (quick_run) 750L else 1000L
# Execution budgets only; the diagnostic gate applies at either budget.
stan_code <- make_stancode(form, data = data, prior = priors)
stopifnot(grepl("log1p_exp", stan_code, fixed = TRUE))
cat("Beta model: generated Stan code validated (softplus precision present).\n")
set.seed(42)
fit <- unwrap_load_fit_cache("periodic_fit", 42L, ITER, WARMUP)
if (is.null(fit)) {
  fit <- brm(form, data = data, prior = priors, backend = "cmdstanr",
    chains = CHAINS, iter = ITER, warmup = WARMUP, cores = CHAINS,
    seed = 42, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95))
  unwrap_save_fit_cache("periodic_fit", fit, 42L, ITER, WARMUP)
}
parameters <- c("b_Intercept", "b_sin24", "b_cos24",
                "b_eta_Intercept", "b_eta_sin24", "b_eta_cos24")
summary_frame <- diagnose_fit(fit, parameters = parameters)
summary_frame

```

```{r}
#| cell-id: "periodic-not-circular-014"
p_trace <- trace_plot(fit, parameters)
save_figure(p_trace, "trace", 9, 6)

```

```{r}
#| cell-id: "periodic-not-circular-015"
# Explicit [grid x draws] linear predictors; no recycled outer callback.
d <- draw_matrix(fit, parameters)
G <- length(time)
lin_mu <- matrix(rep(d$b_Intercept, each = G), nrow = G) +
  outer(sin24, d$b_sin24) + outer(cos24, d$b_cos24)
lin_phi <- matrix(rep(d$b_eta_Intercept, each = G), nrow = G) +
  outer(sin24, d$b_eta_sin24) + outer(cos24, d$b_eta_cos24)
mu_draws <- plogis(lin_mu)
phi_draws <- softplus_stable(lin_phi)
stopifnot(identical(dim(mu_draws), c(G, nrow(d))), identical(dim(phi_draws), dim(mu_draws)))
latent <- rbind(curve_table(mu_draws, mu_true, "mean activity"),
                 curve_table(phi_draws, phi_true, "precision phi"))

p_latent <- latent_curves_plot(time, mu_draws, phi_draws, mu_true, phi_true)
save_figure(p_latent, "periodic_beta_latent_curves", 9, 4)

```

## 3. Reading the figure

The points below are the simulated activity observations. The black line is the median of new activity values drawn from the fitted model at each time. The darker and lighter bands are 50% and 90% highest-density intervals, calculated separately at each time: compact intervals containing those proportions of the simulated predictive values.

This line is a predictive median, not the fitted mean $\mu(t)$. The Beta distribution can be strongly asymmetric, so its median and mean can differ substantially. A predictive median close to 0 or 1 does not imply that the mean activity reaches either endpoint.

Each predictive draw includes variation among observations as well as uncertainty about the fitted coefficients. Consequently, a broad predictive band need not mean that the average activity is poorly known. An afternoon with low average activity can still include occasional high values. Both the changing mean and changing precision affect this spread. Highest-density interval boundaries can also change abruptly as the shape of the distribution changes, even when the underlying mean and precision are smooth.

The model specifies the same activity distribution at 0 and 24 hours. Small differences between plotted summaries at these endpoints can arise from the finite set of predictive draws. The daily cycle joins at midnight; activity remains on its ordinary bounded scale.

This example shows how a periodic predictor can describe a changing distribution of a nonangular outcome. For an animal activity study, the sampling design would guide the choice of cycle length and the treatment of repeated measurements. Additional predictors or hierarchical effects could then describe differences among animals, sites, or days. The likelihood would still follow the type of response being measured. For an applied treatment of daily activity patterns using periodic predictors and hierarchical models, see [Iannarilli et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1111/1365-2656.14213).

**Reference**

Iannarilli, F., Gerber, B. D., Erb, J., and Fieberg, J. R. (2025). A “how-to” guide for estimating animal diel activity using hierarchical models. *Journal of Animal Ecology*, **94**(2), 182–194. [https://doi.org/10.1111/1365-2656.14213](https://doi.org/10.1111/1365-2656.14213).
